newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries close lower, await inflation data.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries close lower, await inflation data.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries closed lower in thin trade Tuesday as players decided to square portfolios ahead of the release of key inflation data over the next two sessions, analysts said.
The 6-1/2-percent 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended down 11/32 at 100-4/32. Its yield rose to 6.49 percent against the 6.46 percent registered at Monday's close.
"It was a pretty quiet session ... the market is just waiting for the inflation numbers," said John Spinello, a managing director at Merrill Lynch.

The Labor Department will release the producer price index (PPI) on Wednesday. The consumer price index (CPI) will be issued on Thursday. Both indicators are for November and will be announced at 0830 EST/1330 GMT.
In a Reuters survey, U.S. analysts expect, on average, overall PPI and CPI to rise 0.3 percent in November.

Analysts said the inflation numbers gained even more importance after Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan said late last week that the Fed must be wary when irrational exuberance affects stocks and assets.
Some Wall Street pundits interpreted Greenspan's words as an indication the Fed chief might be more keen to tighten monetary policy than he was a couple of months ago.
"He might be looking for an excuse ... If the inflation number comes in higher-than-expected that might be it," said the head of the Treasury trading desk at a foreign bank.

Although recent evidence of still tight labor markets appears to give fresh ammunition to those who believe in higher rates, a striking majority of analysts do not expect any change in policy in 1996.
Richard Rippe, Prudential Securities chief economist, said he sees the Fed on hold for "a considerable time," adding he believes that current monetary policy is "mildly restrictive."

The Fed last changed monetary policy in January, when it trimmed its target for the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to the current 5.25 percent. The Fed's policy-setting arm will meet again on December 17.

Some economic indicators released Tuesday were not friendly to the bond market, players said. They expressed some concern about heavy year-end holiday sales after two closely -watched retail indicators came in on the strong side.

The BTM/Schroders chain store sales index rose 1.0 percent in the week ended December 7 versus the prior period. The Lynch, Jones & Ryan Inc Redbook retail sales index rose 0.8 percent in the first fiscal week of December against November.
The market also expressed some disappointment with a smaller-than-expected drop in oil prices after Iraq resumed oil exports on Tuesday.

"For the bond market, it would've been better if prices had dropped further," said a trader at a U.S. investment bank. In afternoon Tuesday trade, the January crude was off 82 cents at $24.48 a barrel.
The year bill rate was up two points at 5.15 percent.

The two-year note closed down 1/32 at 99-27/32, yielding 5.71 percent. The five-year note traded off 5/32 at 99-16/32 to yield 5.99 percent. The ten-year note closed down 9/32 at 102-00, yielding 6.22 percent.

As measured by GovPX, volume was about average at $64.1 billion by late afternoon. GovPX publishes real time Treasury prices and volume from five of the six intra-dealer brokers, representing 65 percent of the intra-dealers trades.
Analysts said flows were fairly quiet on Tuesday. Some minor retail activity was noticed in the morning, but speculators and professional traders dominated the session in the afternoon, they added.
The three-month Treasury bill rate closed flat at 4.82 percent. The six-month bill rate rose two basis points to 4.99 percent.
